items.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002
items.q: And I did and I became like a son to him. He didn’t have any sons, he just had two daughters. And I was brash and I loved him and he took a liking to me and he championed me and taught me a lot.

ctx.x: Yeah. That was the start of how I became so cynical. But I met Lou Donaldson the same way. He just came up to me and asked me to work with him. And he had a steady engagement at a small place in the South Bronx, and he was using an organ. It was an organ trio format. And he asked me to work with him. And I said well look if you’re asking me I’m not about to say no to Donaldson. And I did and I became like a son to him. He didn’t have any sons, he just had two daughters. items.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Herman Foster, Peck. Morrison, and Jimmy Wormworth was the drummer.

ctx.x: So by the time you’d made those first records, you’d been working with him for a year or more.
Yeah. Herman Foster, Peck. Morrison, and Jimmy Wormworth was the drummer. We went up to Buffalo, and hit some of the same clubs. But we had it set up...
That’s when you started establishing that circuit and those relationships.
